title: The snake-catcher
hookLine: a man hauls a frozen dragon into Baghdad, and the sun thaws it (Masnavi 3.976ff)
last: THE WANTING IS THE ANSWER, ARRIVING.

lines: IT WASN'T GONE. IT WAS COLD.
cards: Someone says: oh, I don't really have a temper anymore. Or: I'm totally over that. Or: I could stop anytime.

And as far as they know, it's true. It's been quiet for months. Then comes the holiday with the family, or the bonus check, or the night alone with nothing to do, and there it is again, bigger than before.
It wasn't gone. It was cold. Rumi tells a story about a man who made exactly that mistake, and was the talk of Baghdad for about an hour.

teach.h: A FROZEN DRAGON IN THE SNOW.
teach.b: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. A snake-catcher, a man who made his living catching snakes and showing them off, goes up into the mountains in winter looking for a good one.
He finds a monster: an enormous dragon lying frozen in the snow. It doesn't move. It seems dead.

teach.h: DRAGGED TO BAGHDAD FOR A SHOW.
teach.b: He drags it all the way down to Baghdad to put it on show. Word spreads, and huge crowds come to the riverbank to see it.
He's wrapped it up in ropes and heavy cloth, and he waits for the crowd to grow: more people, more money.

teach.h: THE SUN OF IRAQ WAKES IT.
teach.b: But the sun of Iraq is warm. The cold slowly leaves the dragon's body. It starts to stir.
The ropes snap. The crowd panics and runs, and many are killed in the crush. The snake-catcher stands frozen with fear, and the dragon swallows him.
Then Rumi turns to the reader. Your lower self is that dragon, he says. The Sufi word is nafs: the grasping, angry, hungry part of us.
How could it be dead? It's only frozen, by lack of means, by having no chance to act. Keep it in the snow, Rumi warns.
Don't carry it into the sun of Iraq. The sun is opportunity: money, power, freedom, the right moment. Rumi doesn't say the snake-catcher was evil.
He was proud, a little greedy, and wrong about what was dead. Knowing your dragon isn't shameful. Parading it around thinking it's harmless is where the trouble starts.
Your line: careful in the sun.

how: In Sufi teaching, the nafs, the self that grasps, is watched with care, and this story is told to warn that a desire that seems gone may only be waiting for opportunity.

o: a hunter who kills snakes to keep people safe
a street charmer who tames cobras with a flute
a man who showed off a dragon he thought dead

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: lack of means, keeping it frozen
where the snake-catcher shows it off

s: it was only frozen. the sun woke it.
Rumi says the dragon stands for the nafs, the lower self
frozen by lack of means, not dead.
he was proud, a little greedy, and wrong about what was dead.

games.q: you're the snake-catcher. you've found a huge, frozen dragon in the mountains. it doesn't move. what do you do?
o: drag it to Baghdad and put it on show.
run home and tell no one.
games.why: he drags it to the city for money and fame, and the warm sun brings it back to life.

practice: Ask kindly what's quiet in you only because it hasn't had a chance: a temper, a craving, a grudge, an old habit.
Name it without shame, then ask what sun would wake it: too much money, too little sleep, a certain person, a certain night. Just know it's there.

wordCard.voice: The snake-catcher. A man drags a frozen dragon into Baghdad to show it off, and the warm sun brings it back to life. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a dragon. Rumi's picture of the nafs, the self that grasps.

carryVoice: Your line: careful in the sun. Frozen isn't the same as gone. That's day two hundred four.
